title: Reporters on the Job: From Ely, Minnesota, to Amman, Jordan
text:
Reporters on the Job: From Ely, Minnesota, to Amman, Jordan
Ely, Minn. – Story Hinckley 
Photographers and reporters have different jobs, but producing a story – especially on a reporting trip – requires seamless, often unspoken teamwork. A reporter might put a source at ease while a photographer assesses the light. I’ve always been grateful to photographers who take the wheel of our rental car while I speed-dial elected officials.
That teamwork went into overdrive on a recent trip to Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness with Monitor photography director Alfredo Sosa. We had to do our jobs while paddling and portaging a canoe through a windy rainstorm. When Alfredo needed to photograph the scenery, I steadied our teetering boat and steered us from the rocky shore. Then he took over so I could jot observations on a damp notepad.
This time, teamwork did more than produce a great story. It kept us afloat.
Putney, Vt. – Melanie Stetson Freeman
For a story on turning sheep’s wool into yarn, reporter Kendra Nordin Beato and I traveled to a small spinnery in southeastern Vermont. Kendra called the day before to confirm our tour, but when we arrived, every machine was silent. Nothing was happening. Kendra got what she needed from her interviews, but we wondered why no one had mentioned the shutdown.
You’d be surprised how many times this has happened. Over the years, I’ve learned that assignments rarely go exactly as planned. I’ve arrived at schools only to find them out of session, leaving empty classrooms to photograph. So what’s a photographer to do? Work with what you have. At the spinnery, I photographed the two women Kendra interviewed alongside the idle machinery.
London – Scott Peterson
Dollars fuel a foreign correspondent’s travels. Everything from day rates for translators and drivers to hotel bills requires greenbacks. Surprisingly, in Ukraine, only mint-condition or new $100 bills will do. Any smudge, ink stamp, or minute tear will disqualify a note. Exchange offices 20 miles from the Russian border have refused bills because, they determined, the ink had oxidized and stained the paper.
I returned to London from a recent trip to Ukraine with nearly $3,000 that had been deemed too “dirty,” even for a war-zone country. The irony was that the bank that had originally issued the cash to me in Britain wouldn’t take it all back. When I tried to redeposit it, $300 was deemed “unacceptable” – and had to be spent in the United States. Apparently, even dollars can be refused entry.
Amman, Jordan – Taylor Luck
Reporting from the Middle East takes courage, sound judgment, and an extraordinary network of contacts. But above all, it takes flexibility. Just ask Taylor Luck. Our Middle East correspondent was headed to Saudi Arabia when Houthi strikes shut down the airport. Plan B? A roughly 20-hour drive to Bahrain. Then, heightened U.S. security alerts raised concerns about a wider war with Iran – and the possibility of getting stranded. A reporting trip he was scheduled to lead for me and another editor was canceled, too. In this region, plans can unravel by the hour. What I admire about Taylor is his ability to shrug, regroup, and keep chasing the story, wherever it leads. The best correspondents don’t just adapt to the uncertainty – they find the story in it. – Sara Miller Llana / International editor
